ghaṇṭā
(‘that which makes sound’)
------------------------------------------
Ghaṇṭā or bell is an indispensable part of ritualistic worship. No worship can be started or performed without sounding it first. It is said to embody in itself all the musical instruments. The sound of a bell is प्रणव or ओङ्कार, perceptible to the ears.
It is generally made of bronze.
The body of the bell represents अनन्त (the divinity of time) and the tongue, सरस्वती (the goddess of speech). The handle signifies prāṇaśakti or the energy of प्राण. Usually, the top of the handle is adorned by the images of हनुमान् or गरुड or a चक्र (discus) or नन्दि (the bull-mount of शिव) or a त्रिशूल (trident).
When the bell is sounded in पूजा or worship it is an invitation for the gods to come and a warning for the evil spirits to depart immediately.
The sound of the bell is said to rouse the power of the mantras used in worship. Hence, it is sometimes called ‘mantramātā’ (‘mother of mantras’).
The bell is sounded during पूजा and होम at various stages: आवाहन (inviting the deity), स्नान (giving bath to the image or the symbol), धूप (waving of incense), dīpa (waving of a lighted lamp), at the end of chanting of hymns, पूर्णाहुति (final offering) and so on.
It is the usual practice to hang a bell or a few bells in a temple, in front of the main shrine. Devotees are expected to ring them as they enter.

Ghaṇṭākarṇa
(‘one wearing bells on the ears’)
------------------------------------------
To what ridiculous extent the devotion of a votary towards his इष्टदेवता or chosen deity can go, is illustrated by the story of घण्टाकर्ण. He was a staunch devotee of शिव and an inveterate hater of विष्णु. Not wishing even to listen to the name of विष्णु, he used to hang two bells from his ears, so that their sound could drown the sound of the name of विष्णु if ever uttered by anyone in his presence! However, he is said to have overcome this and become a devotee of विष्णु too, thanks to the intervention of शिव himself.
According to another story, Ghaṇṭa and कर्ण were two rākṣasa brothers who attained salvation by propitiating विष्णु through severe austerities.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa was also the name of a terrible goblin created by शिव to eradicate cutaneous diseases like smallpox. He became, in course of time, a minor village deity, established in a temple of his own and worshipped. By his grace several diseases, especially those born out of sins committed in the previous lives, are cured. His image has 18 hands, holding several articles like वज्र (thunderbolt), sword, discus, arrow, broom, rope, bell, pick-axe and so on.
According to another version in the पुराणस् घण्टाकर्ण was a ghoul, but devoted to विष्णु. He was ultimately saved by कृष्ण.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa is counted among the attendants of स्कन्द (Subrahmaṇya) and also कुबेर, the lord of wealth presiding over the northern quarter.
